The Peri­od­ic Table of Ele­ments lists the 118 chem­i­cal ele­ments that make up every­thing in our world. Some you’re famil­iar with—Hydrogen, Oxy­gen, Nitro­gen, etc. Oth­ers maybe less so—Vanadium, Ger­ma­ni­um, and Yttri­um.
Accord­ing to the Amer­i­can Chem­i­cal Soci­ety, 44 of those 118 ele­ments might dis­ap­pear by cen­tu­ry’s end. Enter the Peri­od­ic Table of Endan­gered Ele­ments (shown above). The most endan­gered ones, high­light­ed in red, are Zinc, Gal­li­um, Ger­ma­ni­um, Arsenic (is this a good or very bad thing?), Sil­ver, Indi­um, Tel­luri­um, and Hafni­um. Made avail­able under a Cre­ative Com­mons license, the Peri­od­ic Table of Endan­gered Ele­ments can be viewed in a larg­er for­mat here.

The orig­i­nal image (top of the page), cre­at­ed in 2015, was updat­ed by EuChemS in 2023 (above). The updat­ed table fea­tures the cur­rent-day avail­abil­i­ty of all 90 ele­ments, rather than just the endan­gered 44 ele­ments, adds an axis for sus­tain­abil­i­ty, and flags ele­ments used in smart­phone pro­duc­tion.

Daily Newsletter
                Lia Strasser on what she got wrong about the AbEx couple, art world homages to Yayoi Kusama, and another museum heist?!
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            As an editor, occasionally a pitch lands in your inbox that makes your heart rate quicken. That’s what I felt when artist and writer Lia Strasser emailed me a few weeks ago, attaching a very personal and moving essay about her relationship to the story of Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock. You may be familiar with the critique that Krasner’s oeuvre has been overshadowed by that of her husband — the alpha male, the household name, the frankly abusive spouse. When Strasser first saw a post announcing The Met’s upcoming exhibition dedicated to both artists, she winced. “Give her a solo show!” Then, Strasser retraced her steps — from the Abstract Expressionist couple’s home in East Hampton to the formative moments that shaped her own artistic identity — and discovered a different reading, one that centers rather than diminishes Krasner’s agency.Also today, the art world pays homage to Yayoi Kusama, who died last week at the age of 97; a Bruges exhibition that claims to de-center Europe fails to live up to its premise; and thieves make off with a diamond necklace from a museum in Vienna.—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

	
		
			What I Got Wrong About Krasner and Pollock
		
	
	
		Earlier this year, the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced its forthcoming exhibition Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous on Instagram, alongside a photograph of the artists by Hans Namuth. Seething, I looked to the comments for affirmation. I didn’t have to scroll for long.

Months earlier, I had visited the Pollock-Krasner House in Springs, East Hampton, knowing far more about Jackson Pollock than I did Lee Krasner. I am a painter myself, and I had come to Springs in the wreck of yet another failed relationship … with a painter. I thought I already knew Krasner’s story. I thought her story was partly my own. | Lia Strasser

title: Pace Gallery Founder Arne Glimcher Criticizes Met Museum Over Planned Galliano Show: Report
description: A range of politicians and public figures have criticized the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York for its forthcoming controversial John Galliano
body:
A range of politicians and public figures have criticized the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York for its forthcoming controversial John Galliano show, including dealer Arne Glimcher, the founder of Pace Gallery, one of the biggest such entreprises in the world.

	A New York Times report published on Friday revealed that the Met has privately faced criticism over the exhibition for Galliano, a fashion designer who was convicted of a hate crime in France in 2011 for antisemitic comments. He later apologized for these comments and went to rehab. He returned to the industry as creative director of Maison Margiela, a role he held from 2014 to 2024.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	The Galliano show is poised to be the Costume Institute‘s big May show for next year. But according to the Times, some have warned that mounting the show in that slot may not be a good decision. 

	As Times reporters Vanessa Friedman and Jacob Bernstein point out, the Met Gala, a highly publicized annual event associated with the Costume Institute’s spring show, is known for taking place on the first Monday in May. Next year, that Monday happens to be Yom HaShoah, otherwise known as Holocaust Remembrance day.

	The Times reported that multiple donors have threatened to rescind or withhold gifts since the announcement of the Galliano show in July. Among those donors, it seems, is Glimcher, who reportedly emailed David Breslin, the Met curator in charge of the modern and contemporary art department, to describe his dissatisfaction.

	“I don’t think you have considered the cost of this action and its reverberations to come,” Glimcher wrote in the email, according to the Times. He went on to write that he and his wife Milly were “seriously reconsidering other works that have been earmarked from our collection to the Met in our wills,” though it was not clear which works those were and whether or not Glimcher had formalized any promised gifts to the museum.

	ARTnews has reached out to Pace Gallery for comment.

	Glimcher has previously donated to the Met, gifting it works by Agnes Martin, Lucas Samara, Robert Mangold, and Mark Rothko over the years. With his son, Marc, and former daughter-in-law, Fairfax Dorn, they donated a 1981 Julian Schnabel painting on the ocassion of the Met’s 150th anniversary. All these artists have long been represented by Pace. 
	

	The Times article also quoted Elisha Wiesel, the daughter of the writer Elie Wiesel, who described the Galliano show as a “pretty bad idea.” The article also mentioned Julie Menin, the speaker of New York’s City Council, who reportedly wrote that the exhibition was “a serious mistake” in a letter addressed to Met director Max Hollein, Costume Institute head Andrew Bolton, and Vogue editorial director Anna Wintour, who has helped shape the Costume Institute into what it is today and is a co-chair of the Met Gala.

	These criticisms have reportedly moved Met board members to discuss the show further. Andrew Solomon, one such board member, told the Times that “confronting cancel culture is a healthier way to go forward than bowing to it.”

	Previously, the Times reported that the Met had conferred with representatives of Jewish groups on the exhibition.

	In a statement to the Times this week, Hollein said, “The Met has no tolerance for antisemitism, racism or prejudice of any kind. We are in close consultation with Jewish leaders and other stakeholders, and we take the concerns we’ve heard very seriously.”

	A Met spokesperson did not immediately respond to ARTnews’s request for comment.

title: 84 Museum Exhibitions and Biennials to See This Fall
description: Want to know which way the winds of the artistic moment are blowing? A reliable way to answer that question is to look at what museums are exhibitin
body:
Want to know which way the winds of the artistic moment are blowing? A reliable way to answer that question is to look at what museums are exhibiting. In the shows on tap for the fall, there’s a clear interest in how best to survive the turbulence and violence in much of the world. “The World-Chaos” is the subtitle given this season to a Kurt Schwitters retrospective at Paris’s Musée Picasso, but it could just as well be applied to shows for Inji Efflatoun, Annemirl Bauer, Marion Wagschal, Ali Cherri, Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian, and Amar Kanwar, all of whom have responded to disturbing displays of power in their own singular ways.
	Other artists have sought visual pleasure in the face of so much chaos. London’s Royal Academy of Arts is mounting a survey of artists’ responses to the French Riviera in the 19th and 20th centuries, Switzerland’s Kunstmuseum Bern is surveying European artist colonies during an overlapping time period, and Helsinki’s Ateneum Art Museum is exhibiting Nordic women’s spiritualist art of the era. But sometimes, rich colors and extravagant abstraction are not enough; the career of Franz Marc, a German Expressionist who was killed in battle during World War I, proves as much. His work is being given the retrospective treatment at the K20 museum in Düsseldorf.
	Perhaps the dour mood of the present is what has caused so many shows to turn to the past, often with a revisionist gaze. The São Paulo Museum of Art is continuing its wonderful “Historiás” series, this time with a focus on Latin America, and Oslo’s National Museum is bringing to the fore female Old Masters whom the canon has largely ignored. MUDAM in Luxembourg is taking a look at Japanese women artists from the postwar era, Milan’s Fondazione Prada will view antiquity through a globalist lens, and the Palazzo Strozzi in Florence has an exhibition of broken artworks from years past. Fragmentary though they may be, these pieces are a lot of fun to view.
	Below, a look at 84 museum exhibitions and biennials to see this fall.

			
			
	“Ragnar Kjartansson: Politics of the Obvious” at Buffalo AKG Art Museum, New York
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy the artist; Luhring Augustine, New York; and i8, Reykjavik				
					
				

	The art world tends not to agree on much, but few would disparage Ragnar Kjartansson’s The Visitors (2012), a video installation in which a troupe of musicians play their somber song together, each from a different room in a dilapidated house. Upon its debut, the work was immediately celebrated as a powerful piece about the frailty of human relations; it is now considered a classic. The Visitors will appear in this survey of the Icelandic artist’s work, which frequently takes the form of slow-paced videos in which banal acts take place over prolonged periods. The latest work to continue that theme is Sundays Without Love (2025), which brings to life a postcard of a countryside scene that Kjartansson keeps on his fridge.

	September 3–January 31, 2027

		
			
			
	“Latin American Histories” at São Paulo Museum of Art
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy MASP				
					
				

	This institution’s “Historiás” exhibition series has lived up to its name by drawing under-recognized art histories into the canon. Having previously tackled subjects such as Black Atlantic culture, indigenous rights, and environmentalism, the series is now turning its focus local, relatively speaking. “Latin American Histories” directs its attention to the entire region of which Brazil is a part, examining topics from Baroque art to the oppression of indigenous people to the Zapatista movement. Curators Amanda Carneiro and Julieta González have deliberately cast a wide net, viewing the region’s history as a collision of many narratives rather than a single cohesive story.

	September 4–January 13, 2027

		
			
			
	Gwangju Biennale at Various venues, Gwangju, South Korea
			
										
					Image Credit: Photo Jung Yeon-Je/AFP via Getty Images				
					
				

	Rainer Maria Rilke concluded one famed poem with the line “You must change your life,” but he didn’t exactly provide an instructional manual for how to fulfill his directive. Taking that line as its inspiration, this edition of Asia’s top biennial suggests that there are infinite ways to meet Rilke’s demand, which is really about the many means by which one can reimagine oneself for the better. Artist Ho Tzu Nyen, the biennial’s curator, has amassed a list of 43 participants whose work can be seen as bearing this out. Those artists include an array of stars—among them the Indian photographer Sohrab Hura, a current participant in the Venice Biennale—as well as other, more mysterious participants, including one billed only as the Volcanoes of Jeju, a reference to the natural fissures off the coast of a South Korean island.

	September 5–November 15

		
			
			
	“Koo Jeong A: OUSSSMOS” at Leeum Museum of Art, Seoul
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Koo Jeong A/Kunsthaus Bregenz/Photo Markus Tretter/Courtesy the artist				
					
				

	A few years ago, Koo Jeong A put out a query that was disseminated widely: “What is your scent memory of Korea?” On the basis of the 600 responses they received, Koo created a “scent landscape” for the Venice Biennale’s Korean Pavilion; it smelled woody, perhaps also a bit like mothballs. For Koo, the project was about trying to visualize the invisible, a theme they have considered in many sleek installations, and one they will continue to mull with this Leeum Museum show, which continues their “OUSSSMOS” installation series. Included here will be a newly commissioned work called [MOBIOUSSS], which a press release enigmatically describes as a “monumental luminous structure that evokes both the symbol of infinity and a skatepark.”

	September 5–December 27

		
			
			
	“Ali Cherri: Soul Witness” at WIELS Contemporary Art Centre, Brussels
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy the artist and Almine Rech				
					
				

	Ali Cherri has referred to his films contemplating wartime carnage and traumatic memories as “landscapes of violence.” Born in Lebanon and based in Paris and Beirut, Cherri infuses these films with surrealism, drifting in and out of dreams and often obscuring whether these works are set in the past or present. (To further the confusion, he makes sculptures that appear to have been created by bygone empires of the Middle East and Egypt.) The winner of the 2022 Venice Biennale’s award for a promising young artist, Cherri will here display an array of these films, including The Sentinel (2026), in which a French soldier shoots himself somewhere along the northern edge of Cyprus, then drifts around a set of ruins.

	September 5–January 3, 2027

		
			
			
	Ismael Nery at Pinacoteca de São Paulo
			
										
					Image Credit: Isabella Matheus/Pinacoteca de São Paulo/Collection of the José and Paulina Nemirovsky Foundation, on loan to the Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo				
					
				

	Unlike many other Brazilian modernists, Ismael Nery never entirely abandoned the human figure. But his people did not look like those you might see on the street: Nery’s sometimes had multiple faces and mismatched eyes. Occasionally, it wasn’t easy to tell where these people ended and the backgrounds behind them began, and frequently, Nery made their gender ambiguous—a gesture that feels particularly au courant today. Having appeared in the 2024 Venice Biennale, which was that year organized by the celebrated Brazilian curator Adriano Pedrosa, Nery is now getting an expansive survey in his homeland.

	September 5–January 31, 2027

		
			
			
	“Annemirl Bauer: A Rapture in the World” at Das Minsk, Potsdam, Germany
			
										
					Image Credit: ©2025 VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn/Annemirl Bauer Archive				
					
				

	Annemirl Bauer’s name is likely to be unfamiliar to most people, even within Germany, and there are clear reasons why. During the 1980s, while working in East Germany, she spoke out against the requirement that women serve in the military; she also agitated for citizens of the GDR to be allowed to travel without restrictions. These protests gained Bauer the attention of the authorities, who began to surveil her. She died at the age of 50 in 1989, less than two months before the fall of the Berlin Wall; by that point she had built up a significant oeuvre of paintings and drawings that explicitly critiqued the constraints placed on East Germans like herself. At long last, she is getting a proper retrospective within Germany.

	September 5–February 7, 2027

		
			
			
	“Maverick Kings: Three Visionary Pharaohs of Egypt’s Golden Age” at Museum of Fine Arts Boston
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Museum of Fine Arts Boston				
					
				

	The question of how art can be used to enhance power is one that occupies rulers, presidents, and prime ministers today, but in fact that query is thousands of years old. While it did not begin in ancient Egypt, it was certainly in play during the 18th Dynasty (ca. 1550–1292 BCE), when three pharaohs—Hatshepsut, Amenhotep III, and Akhenaten—grew increasingly adept at using sculpture to impress their authority upon the masses. This show centers on that trio and includes a range of statues of Akenhaten, who had a predilection for objects that portrayed him with almond-shaped eyes and an elongated head. These reliefs and statues are otherworldly, off-putting, and undeniably singular.

	September 6–December 6

		
			
			
	“Hikmah” at Center for Contemporary Arts Tashkent, Uzbekistan
			
										
					Image Credit: Christopher Snee/©Art Gallery of New South Wales/Courtesy Kimsooja Studio				
					
				

	Central Asia’s art scene has experienced a seismic shift in the past couple of years, thanks to the introduction of a new biennial in Bukhara and a range of new art spaces in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The newest of these institutions is the Centre for Contemporary Art Tashkent, whose inaugural show is “Hikmah,” a group exhibition whose name means “wisdom” in Uzbek. Mulling the transmission of ideas and the acquisition of knowledge, the show will feature an array of international artists, among them Tarik Kiswanson, a Paris-based sculptor whose work has explored his family’s Palestinian heritage and the movements of people across the globe.

	September 6–January 31, 2027

		
			
			
	Counterpublic at Various Venues, St. Louis, Missouri
			
										
					Image Credit: Photo Izaiah Johnson				
					
				

	The first edition of this triennial, in 2023, appears to have made a lasting impact on St. Louis, where some of its commissions remain viewable today. That makes Counterpublic one of the few biennial-style shows to be more than a parachute-in exhibition and offers a reason to keep tabs on the second edition, curated by Jordan Carter, Raphael Fonseca, Stefanie Hessler, Nora N. Khan, and Wanda Nanibush. Under the theme of “Coyote Time,” the exhibition is devoted to the notion of uncertainty and features artists such as Rebecca Belmore, Li Yi-Fan, and Ximena Garrido-Lecca. One of its more exciting offerings is a show within a show: a multi-museum survey for Juanita McNeely, whose figurative paintings examine misogynistic violence in all its grotesqueness.

	September 10–December 13

		
			
			
	“Kreuzberg: Art and Migration Since 1960” at Gropius Bau, Berlin
			
										
					Image Credit: Hafid Lhachmi/Courtesy the Estate; Kalfayan Galleries, Athens and Thessaloniki; and Peter Kilchmann, Zurich				
					
				

	Ayşe Erkmen’s Am Haus (1994), a set of 40 Turkish-language suffixes that are permanently arrayed across the facade of a building in Berlin’s Kreuzberg district, is a gesture both subtle and impactful. Erkmen has noted that the work is legible only to those who speak Turkish, so that “the so-called outsider in German society becomes the insider.” Indeed, Kreuzberg is an artist-friendly neighborhood with a history of acting as a home to a large immigrant community. This exhibition, a celebration of Kreuzberg’s ability to turn outsiders into insiders, will present 100 works by migrants who have passed through the district, among them artists Colette Lumiere, Aykan Safoğlu, and Eduardo Arroyo.

	September 10–January 17, 2027

		
			
			
	“Ayana Evans: Nobody’s Gonna Love You the Way I Do” at Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis
			
										
					Image Credit: Dominique Durouseau and Nyugen Smith				
					
				

	When she appears in public, Ayana Evans often wears a bright green catsuit that is hard to miss. Such a gesture is of a piece with her performances, which are about drawing attention to Black womanhood and all the ideas attached to it. “She makes herself hypervisible,” the critic Seph Rodney once wrote. “Her black body cannot, and will not, be ignored or brushed aside.” Having staged memorable works that have variously involved doing jumping jacks for hours on end and wearing a sign that read “I JUST CAME HERE TO FIND A HUSBAND,” Evans will now bring her practice within museum walls in a show billed as her first survey. Included will be video and photographic documentation as well as eye-catching clothes that can be donned by attendees wishing to make themselves hypervisible as well.

	September 10–February 7, 2027

		
			
			
	“Maurizio Cattelan: NIGHT” at Neue Nationalgalerie, Berlin
			
										
					Image Credit: Paolo Pellion di Persona/Courtesy Castello di Rivoli				
					
				

	The Preis der Nationalgalerie, one of Berlin’s top art awards, typically goes to an artist under the age of 40 based in the German capital. It was a surprise, then, when Maurizio Cattelan, a prankster artist in his mid-60s who was neither born nor based in Berlin, won the prize in 2025. Maybe that’s why the Neue Nationalgalerie has gone to great lengths to attribute a vague sense of Germanness to the Italian Cattelan, whom the institution notes has curated one edition of the Berlin Biennale and created one unforgettable Germany-themed sculpture: Him (2001), a tiny, penitent Adolf Hitler. Him is one of the artworks featured in this exhibition, which will also feature a new piece that the museum has called “a far-reaching intervention into the museum’s spatial framework.” That’s a pretty anodyne description for work by an artist known for duct-taping a banana to a wall and calling it art.

	September 10–March 7, 2027

		
			
			
	“The Bayeux Tapestry” at British Museum, London
			
										
					Image Credit: Loic Venance/AFP via Getty Images				
					
				

	Sometimes, one work is enough to be an exhibition unto itself. Such is the case here, in this once-in-a-lifetime presentation of the Bayeux Tapestry, a 230-foot-long embroidered textile made between 1070 and 1082 that narrates the events leading up to the Norman Conquest of England. Typically housed at the Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux in France, the work has not visited the United Kingdom in roughly a millennium. That makes the loan extraordinary. It’s also extraordinarily valuable—insured at $1.5 million—because of its historical significance: The tapestry pioneered a new way of telling history by serializing its embroidered images, each of which is remarkably detailed.

	September 10–July 11, 2027

		
			
			
	“Marion Wagschal: Cyclops and Other Tales” at National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Marion Wagschal/Courtesy the artist/Private collection				
					
				

	In her 1980–2013 painting Tales from the Schwarzwald as Told by My Mother, Marion Wagschal renders a cascade of translucent figures interrupted by a thronelike chair, a mushroom, and leafy trees. Though it may seem to be Wagschal’s fantastical invention, the painting is meant to depict stories about Germany’s Black Forest that were imparted to the artist by her parents, who survived the Holocaust and moved to Trinidad and Tobago, where Wagschal was born in 1943. The painting demonstrates Wagschal’s acute ability to show how history morphs, growing stranger as it is told and retold. Having gained a cult following in Canada, where she has been based since the 1950s, Wagschal will now have a retrospective that examines the role of secondhand trauma in her art.

	September 11–January 17, 2027

		
			
			
	“Franz Marc: The Quest for a Better World” at K20, Düsseldorf
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza, Madrid				
					
				

	The German modernist painter Franz Marc assigned meaning to each of the bright hues he used in his landscapes. “Blue is the male principle, astringent and spiritual,” he once said. “Yellow is the female principle, gentle, gay and spiritual. Red is matter, brutal and heavy and always the color to be opposed and overcome by the other two.” The artist combined those colors in pastoral scenes that exhibited a unique sense of harmony; they made him one of the primary artists of the Blaue Reiter movement of the 1910s. How Marc achieved that harmony before his untimely demise—he died at 36 while fighting in the Battle of Verdun—is the subject of this retrospective, billed as the first significant show devoted to the artist in two decades.

	September 12–January 24, 2027

		
			
			
	“The Technologies of Peace: Art and Transition in Contemporary Europe (1989 – 2026)” at Irish Museum of Modern Art, Dublin
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy the artist				
					
				

	Protests in support of liberation are often accompanied by calls for solidarity, which is likely why this show includes artists from Yugoslavia, Poland, Greece, Catalonia, Slovenia, and other European locales that have faced periods of turmoil in the past 35 years. But rather than lingering on the trauma associated with upheaval, this show focuses on peacetime and the way artists have envisioned it. With an artist list spanning artists as diverse as Kosovar sculptor Petrit Halilaj and the Eurasian art collective Slavs and Tatars, the exhibition implicitly shows that one community’s afflictions are never meant to be solved alone.

	September 12–May 9, 2027

		
			
			
	“Remedios Varo: Painting Magic” at Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, Humlebaek, Denmark
			
										
					Image Credit: Colección FEMSA/©2026 Remedios Varo/VISDA
				
					
				

	There’s a tendency to call Surrealist art “dreamlike.” But that word would probably not have pleased Remedios Varo, the Spanish-born Mexican artist whose paintings of witchy figures conspiring in settings recalling cloisters and laboratories stand as some of the weirdest works of the 20th century. “The dream world and the real world are the same,” she once said of these paintings, which conjure rituals that exist outside the realm of reason. Once an obscure figure at the fringes of Surrealism studies, Varo has gained a large following over the past decade, and that is likely to make this retrospective, the biggest devoted to her in some time, a hit with scholars and new initiates alike.

	September 18–January 10, 2027

		
			
			
	“Simone Fattal: From Cities at the Bottom of the Lake” at Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris
				

	Born in Syria and based for much of her career in the United States and France, Simone Fattal is known for sculptures that obliquely evoke the distant past: Adam and Eve (2021), a work that appeared at the 2022 Venice Biennale, depicted the biblical couple by way of two leggy figures without arms or facial features. While sculptures like these have in recent years been exhibited internationally, the rest of Fattal’s practice remains less widely known. This 100-work retrospective aims to remedy that with landscape paintings from early in her career, when she was still based in Beirut; writings published through her now-defunct Post-Apollo Press; and objects related to collaborations with Etel Adnan, the late painter and poet who was Fattal’s romantic partner.

	September 18–January 24, 2027

		
			
			
	“Picasso – Bacon: What It Feels Like to Be Human” at Albertina Museum, Vienna
			
										
					Image Credit: ©The Estate of Francis Bacon, All rights reserved/Bildrecht, Vienna und DACS, London 2026/Neue Nationalgalerie, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin				
					
				

	“Flesh and meat are life,” the painter Francis Bacon once said. This view certainly showed in his art, which often featured people posed among carcasses; at times, his sitters themselves resembled raw meat, their faces appearing battered or carved. The tendency to view humans in this way also extended to one of Bacon’s main inspirations, Pablo Picasso, who gained fame—and, in some feminist corners, notoriety—for paintings that render bodies so abstract that they appear not to even belong to people. This 70-work show of Picasso and Bacon paintings elucidates a violent tendency running across their oeuvres that has been both hard to pin down and tough to swallow.

	September 18–January 31, 2027

		
			
			
	“Clare Rojas: Returning” at Colombus Museum of Art, Ohio
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy the artist, Jessica Silverman Gallery, and Andrew Kreps Gallery				
					
				

	This exhibition is aptly titled, since painter Clare Rojas recently came back to her home state of Ohio after a prolonged period in California’s Bay Area, where she achieved fame during the 1990s. (The show’s city is also fitting: Rojas was born in Columbus.) Her art is, in a way, about how individuals relate to the environments that produce them, with abstracted birds and flowers recurring throughout her lush paintings. Perhaps somewhat relatedly, the release for the show notes that Rojas recently planted California poppies in the garden of her Ohio home.

	September 18–February 7, 2027

		
			
			
	Taryn Simon at Guggenheim Museum, New York
			
										
					Image Credit: ©2026 Taryn Simon				
					
				

	“I don’t think I’ve ever enjoyed the making of my work,” Taryn Simon once said. “It’s a labor.” It’s no surprise she feels this way, given that her work has addressed topics such as wrongful incarceration, genocide, grief, and the fragility of democracy, often with a rigor that is rare among artists, even in a time when research-oriented art is widely exhibited. Using photography as her primary medium, she has frequently directed her attention toward America’s hidden histories, which may be one reason the Guggenheim chose Simon to fill its rotunda as the nation’s 250th anniversary year draws to a close. Though the actual contents of the show remain undisclosed, the museum has described the exhibition as “a massive constellation of images around a sweeping narrative that spirals through the space.”

	September 18–March 14, 2027

		
			
			
	John Baldessari at UCCA Center for Contemporary Art, Beijing

	October 17–January 10, 2027

		
			
			
	“Imaginary Engine: From Masterpieces of the Collection Renault to Artists of Today” at Large, Paris
			
										
					Image Credit: Aurélien Mole/©Zhenya Machneva and Galerie Georges-Philippe et Nathalie Vallois/ADAGP, Paris				
					
				

	For two decades, collectors have been trying to open an art museum in a former Renault car factory on Île Seguin, an island in the River Seine; Laurent Dumas has finally succeeded where others before him have failed. Dumas’s museum, Le Large, comes with more than 250,000 square feet of exhibition space, and if its inaugural exhibition is any indication, its ambitions are equally, well, large. Cecilia Alemani, the curator of the acclaimed 2022 Venice Biennale, has been tapped to do the opening show, which broadly considers the notion of machinery across recent art history. The show will feature works from Renault’s collection alongside new commissions from artists such as Théo Mercier, Thu Van Tran, and Bertrand Lavier.

	October 17–March 7, 2027

		
			
			
	“Myths and Monsters: The Art of Fantasy in Asia” at M+, Hong Kong
			
										
					Image Credit: MMCA, Seoul				
					
				

	M+’s offerings tend to bring artworks into dialogue with non-artworks, and this show focused on fictional universes and fearsome creatures is no different in that regard. It’s being teased with a painting from the 1950s by Kim YoungHwan, who was aligned with a Korean strain of Surrealism. But the museum’s press materials suggest that one will also find haute couture, video games, and ephemera related to popular TV shows. Reaching back even farther in time, there will also be ukiyo-e woodblock prints, Tibetan Buddhist scrolls, and a whole lot more.

	October 17–April 4, 2027

		
			
			
	“The Brockman Gallery: Los Angeles, 1967–1990” at Los Angeles County Museum of Art
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Tami Outterbridge/Estate of John Outterbridge, image courtesy parrasch heijnen, Los Angeles/Collection of Linda F. Beal				
					
				

	Without Los Angeles’s Brockman Gallery, there might be no David Hammons—he had his first solo show there in 1971, then went on to achieve acclaim. Likewise John Outterbridge, Noah Purifoy, and a host of others who passed through the gallery, which was essential in fostering more than one generation of Black artists before the mainstream commercial system embraced them. Founded by artist Alonzo Davis and his brother Dale, the Brockman Gallery was a rarity in its time: Artist Ulysses Jenkins, who worked there for two years, recalled it as one of the few places he knew of that supported Black art. Now it is celebrated in this exhibition, which includes works by Hammons, Suzanne Jackson, Carrie Mae Weems, and others with Brockman ties.

	October 18–January 24, 2027

		
			
			
	“The Freudian Universe of Dalí” at Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum, Madrid
			
										
					Image Credit: Scala/Dig. Image MoMA, New York				
					
				

	Never mind that Salvador Dalí and Sigmund Freud met only once, in 1938, and never mind that their encounter didn’t go so well, with the famed psychoanalyst saying of Dalí’s art, “In classic paintings I look for the unconscious, but in your paintings I look for the conscious.” (Dalí was visibly unappreciative of Freud’s response, leading Freud to term him a “fanatic.” Ouch!) This show proposes that Freud’s theories are one key to unraveling the mysteries of Dalí’s Surrealist paintings, which are famously rife with references to sexual hang-ups and psychological torment. Alongside Dalí’s work, the show will also feature pieces by others inspired by what the museum calls “Freudian thought,” among them Gino Severini, Pablo Picasso, and Jean Arp.

	October 20–January 24, 2027

		
			
			
	Leonor Fini at Schirn Kunsthalle, Frankfurt, Germany
			
										
					Image Credit: Galerie Minsky, Paris/©2026 VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn/Private Collection				
					
				

	Even by the standards of the Surrealist cohort, Leonor Fini produced paintings that were transgressive, filled as they were with images of androgynous people, bodacious sphinxes, flipped power dynamics, and sexual subversion. (The artist, who was openly bisexual, bucked what was expected of women during her day in her personal life as well.) Born in Argentina and based for much of her career in France, Fini made art so ahead of its time that it can be difficult to remember that it’s roughly a century old. And yet, it is a blast from the past, in part because Fini looked toward art history for inspiration. This 100-work show demonstrates how she drew liberally from art of the Renaissance, German Romanticism, Symbolism, and other movements and remade it anew.

	October 23–February 21, 2027

		
			
			
	“Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism” at Ateneum Art Museum, Helsinki
			
										
					Image Credit: Hannu Pakarinen/Ateneum Art Museum				
					
				

	Tapping a modish fascination with spiritualist women, this exhibition surveys an array of female artists from the Nordic region who have looked beyond our world to engage with mysterious beings in other realms. Beginning in the 19th century and continuing to the present day, the show includes such artists as Rita Kernn-Larsen, a Danish Surrealist who painted hallucinatory nudes; Anna-Eva Bergman, a Swedish painter of luminous abstractions who drew her inspiration from the landscape around her; and Outi Pieski, a Sámi artist from Finland whose sprawling installations frequently enlist yarn and draw on craft traditions known as duodji.

	October 23–February 28, 2027

		
			
			
	Rosalie Gascoigne at National Gallery of Australia, Canberra
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Rosalie Gascoigne/Copyright Agency/National Gallery of Australia				
					
				

	Though she is now considered one of the most important artists in recent Australian art history, Rosalie Gascoigne had a slow start—she did not exhibit her assemblages of tossed-off objects until the 1970s, when she was in her mid-50s. But after she began showing these works, critics could not get enough of them; an appearance at the Venice Biennale came in 1982. Born in New Zealand and based in Canberra, Gascoigne gathered objects that most might consider junk—scrap wood, old wheels, dirty dolls—and asked how they retained the memories of the places from which they had come. Gascoigne, who died in 1999, said that she was trying to “recall the feeling of an actual moment in the landscape.” This retrospective will explore how she succeeded in doing so.

	October 24–February 14, 2027

		
			
			
	Wilhelmina Barns-Graham at Tate St. Ives, England
			
										
					Image Credit: Andy Phillipson/Livewire Image/©Wilhelmina Barns-Graham Trust				
					
				

	Though Wilhelmina Barns-Graham often looked to the British landscape for inspiration, the abstractions that resulted typically did not resemble natural formations of any kind. This was, of course, the point: Barns-Graham said she wanted to explore the relationship between one’s interiority and the outside world, once noting that her process was one of “looking in / looking out.” Barns-Graham has always been esteemed by enthusiasts of British modernism, but she has never gotten a proper retrospective until this one, which includes a whopping 170 works. It is fittingly being staged in St Ives, the British city where the Scottish-born artist spent the formative years of her career.

	October 24–May 3, 2027

		
			
			
	“Gardar Eine Einarsson: The Purpose of a System Is What It Does” at Kode Bergen Art Museum, Norway
			
										
					Image Credit: Stein Jørgenssen/©Gardar Eine Einarsson/BONO 2026/Collection of Erling Kagge				
					
				

	Think of Gardar Eide Einarsson as a heavy-metal Cady Noland. Like her, he makes sleek installations referencing distinctly American subjects, such as police violence and national pride. (American flags devoid of color recur in the work he’s made since moving from his homeland of Norway to the United States on September 10, 2001, the day before the Twin Towers fell.) Also like Noland, Einarsson revisits the legacy of Minimalism, using pared-down symbols and images to suggest that the movement was really all about asserting an uneven power dynamic. Einarsson’s work has a heart of darkness that is virtually unparalleled; whether you like his art or not, that makes him stand out. Whether it is too dark, even in these dark times, is something worth considering while visiting this 125-work show, Einarsson’s first major survey in the country where he was born.

	October 29–February 27, 2027

		
			
			
	“Marisa Merz: La danza delle ore (The Dance of the Hours)” at Castello di Rivoli, Fondazione Merz, and Galleria Civica d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea di Torino, Turin
			
										
					Image Credit: Renato Ghiazza/Courtesy Fondazione Merz				
					
				

	To sum up Marisa Merz’s practice in one sentence feels unfair, so we won’t even try. Here, instead, is a brief list of some things she produced: knots of hemp tied to a wire mesh, installations formed from suspended pieces of aluminum, self-portraits without any recognizable features, little busts that look less like human heads than animal parts. Some have lumped this Italian sculptor, who died in 2019, with Arte Povera, but her art doesn’t quite fit with that 1960s movement or, really, any other concurrent one. The feverish bursts of creativity she unleashed cannot be contained by one retrospective, which may be the reason three institutions banded together to mount a single show. The exhibition will also feature pieces by artists whose work dialogues nicely with Merz’s, including Solange Pessoa, Lara Favaretto, and Miriam Cahn.

	October 29–April 4, 2027 (all venues)

		
			
			
	“Journey into Freedom. Capri – Skagen – Monte Verità” at Kunstmuseum Bern, Switzerland
			
										
					Image Credit: Museumsberg Flensburg				
					
				

	Many artists throughout time have periodically felt a burning desire to escape the claustrophobic confines of their studio for somewhere more picturesque. This exhibition proposes that the tendency was particularly pronounced between 1830 and 1930, when European painters fled their homes for artist colonies that ended up spurring new styles. One such colony was in Skagen, in the north of Denmark. During the 19th century, that seaside town became the meeting point for an array of Scandinavians, among them the Norwegian painter Christian Krohg, whose time in Skagen turned his style gritty and unsentimental as he began to focus on local fishermen and peasants.

	October 30–January 31, 2027

		
			
			
	“Mariko Mori: All That Shines” at Mori Art Museum, Tokyo
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy the artist				
					
				

	In 1994, Mariko Mori boarded the Tokyo subway wearing a silvery dress that made her look like a cyborg. Photographs of this action, a performance of sorts, emphasize the otherworldliness of Mori’s outfit—and the leering gazes of the men around her. The piece stands in well for Mori’s practice, which has seen the artist consider why Japan of the present day finds itself so occupied with the futuristic female form. With fembots and female AI assistants now the stuff of everyday life, the Mori Art Museum is appropriately giving a retrospective to Mori this season. Included will be Wave UFO (1999–2002), a flying saucer–like sculpture that viewers can enter; inside, they can hook themselves up to equipment that interprets their brain waves.

	October 31–March 28, 2027

		
			
			
	“Séraphine Louis: De Senlis et sans rivale” at Centre Pompidou-Metz, France
			
										
					Image Credit: ©2026 Digital image, The Museum of Modern Art, New York/Scala, Florence				
					
				

	Séraphine Louis’s life was about as colorful as her paintings. While working as a housekeeper for families in the French town of Senlis, this self-taught artist began producing mystifying still lifes featuring plants and bowls that burst with leaves and fruit. In these often otherworldly paintings observers have found a spiritual quality that some have attributed to her Christian faith; others have analyzed them through the lens of her psychological profile: She had bouts of paranoia and spent the last decade of her life in a psychiatric hospital. But such a reading deprives these works of their edge. For full effect, they require a retrospective like this one, which will synthesize Louis’s eventful life story with her equally rich art.

	October 31–April 12, 2027

		
			
			
	“Hard Art” at MoMA PS1, New York
			
										
					Image Credit: Thomas Barratt/Courtesy the artist and Petzel, New York				
					
				

	The painter Peter Bradley once said that when it comes to abstraction, “the colors and shapes of the paintings . . . are seen in our daily lives.” What might it mean, then, for an artist like Bradley to invoke the colors associated with Blackness? That query guides this ambitious survey, which establishes a lineage of 40 Black artists working in abstraction that includes Bradley, Melvin Edwards, Barbara Chase-Riboud, and other giants of the 1960s and ’70s alongside younger talents like Carolyn Lazard, Aria Dean, and SoiL Thornton. Though touted as a painting show, the exhibition’s star work may be a sculpture: Torkwase Dyson, an artist known for her gigantic installations composed of arcing black forms, has been commissioned to create a new work responding to the concept of Black liberation.

	Opens November 5

		
			
			
	“Global Antiquity” at Fondazione Prada, Milan
			
										
					Image Credit: Dmytro Klochko/National Museum of the History of Ukraine				
					
				

	Recent exhibitions have revisited the notion of ancient empires, showing that they were more sprawling than many realize. For example, the Met’s memorable 2023 exhibition “Africa & Byzantium” explored how ancient Greece’s tendrils reached Egypt, Ethiopia, and other nations. Building on the legacy of that scholarship is this exhibition, which will place Greco-Roman artifacts in the context of objects from China, India, and elsewhere. The Fondazione Prada has a taste for exhibitions with an edge, and this one continues that sensibility. Rather than situating its array of works in traditional galleries, as most museums would, this show will be staged in what the Fondazione Prada has called a “set,” designed by the architect Renzo Piano.

	November 5–March 1, 2027

		
			
			
	Franz West at Albertina Modern and Wien Museum, Vienna
			
										
					Image Credit: Albertina Museum, Vienna				
					
				

	Legend has it that, in 1968, at a University of Vienna event that featured a range of outré performances by the Actionists, the artist Franz West led the crowd in applauding works that many considered offensive. Such a gesture put West on the right side of art history—the Actionists are now canonized—and helped render him a central figure of the Austrian art scene, a reputation he would continue to hold until his death in 2012. Known for large-scale sculptures that trouble the division between art and design while also jokingly needling the merits of functionalism, West will be posthumously feted on what would have been his 80th birthday with two concurrent shows in Vienna. At the Albertina, West is receiving a conventional retrospective in one of the city’s great museums. Meanwhile, the Wien Museum is focusing on West’s deep connections to Vienna, with an emphasis on documentation related to his site-specific sculptures.

	November 6–March 29, 2027 (Albertina); November 6–May 2, 2027 (Wien)

		
			
			
	“Laurent Grasso: Metaphysical Maze” at MASS MoCA, North Adams, Massachusetts
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Laurent Grasso / ADAGP, Paris, 2025/Courtesy the artist, Sean Kelly, and Perrotin				
					
				

	While UFOlogists continue to puzzle over a tranche of files released by the Pentagon earlier this summer, one U.S. museum is devoting an entire structure to a show whose centerpiece will contend with the existence of aliens. Laurent Grasso, a winner of the Prix Marcel Duchamp, will here debut Cosmic Time, a film he made following collaborations with scientists at the SETI Institute. Grasso has not released details about the film, but he’s described it as being about “invisible forces that are often difficult to grasp.” Surrounding it will be other works by Grasso, who will not provide explanatory labels for them in an attempt to enhance their mystery.

	November 7–January 16, 2028

		
			
			
	“Impressionism: Artists, Dealers, Collectors” at Museum Barberini, Potsdam, Germany
			
										
					Image Credit: Hasso Plattner Collection				
					
				

	It took a lot of guts for the Impressionists to defy the artistic conventions of the French art world—and it took some great art dealers to help their work weather a critical firestorm and enter the annals of art history. Rather than charting the movement’s rise through the contributions of artists such as Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, and Camille Pissarro, this exhibition focuses on the art market that upheld them. Paul Durand-Ruel, whose Paris gallery gave formative shows to Monet and Édouard Manet, is an obvious protagonist in that narrative, but the show will also place due emphasis on less well-known collectors like Jean-Baptiste Faure, an opera singer who acquired works by Manet, Monet, and Edgar Degas that now reside in the collections of major museums across the globe.

	November 7–February 21, 2027

		
			
			
	“Aage Gaup: Sculpting a Return/Hábmet máhccama” at Moderna Museet, Stockholm
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Aage Gaup				
					
				

	Sámi art, long relegated to the margins of Nordic art history, has gradually gained mainstream attention, making appearances at some of the world’s biggest museums and biennials. One recurrent figure in those presentations is Aage Gaup, a sculptor, set designer, and member of the Máze Group, a collective of artists that, during the 1970s, showed future generations what Sámi collectivity could look like. Like many Sámi people of his era, Gaup was legally forced into a childhood education that bore no relation to his Sámi ways; he spent a career rekindling his relationship to Sápmi, its culture, and its lore via his art. Many of his spare sculptures thus evoke Sápmi’s landscape, tenderly alluding to its hills and fields by way of arcs of wood.

	November 11–January 24, 2027

		
			
			
	“Abbas Akhavan: Variations on a Garden” at Walker Art Center, Minneapolis
			
										
					Image Credit: David Stjernholm				
					
				

	At the current Venice Biennale, Abbas Akhavan is representing Canada with an installation that transforms the nation’s pavilion into a terrarium-like space. Inside, water lilies are growing from seeds transported from England. This transnational way of working is typical for the Iran-born artist, whose installations consider what happens when objects and people travel—and what gets lost in the process. With his star at its height, Akhavan will receive a survey that will include installations enlisting such materials as soil and water.

	November 12–April 18, 2027

		
			
			
	Lagos Biennial at Various venues, Lagos, Nigeria
				

	West Africa will have a strong biennial season this fall, with the Dak’Art biennial in Dakar and the Lagos Biennial happening concurrently. (The Dakar event remained undetailed at press time.) The Lagos Biennial, for its part, is titled “The Museum of Things Unseen”; the show will feature artists whose work pays mind to the complex array of market and institutional forces that shape the art world. Furen Dai, Chinyere Obieze, and Sam Hopkins are curating the show, whose artist list has not yet been released.

	November 14–December 6

		
			
			
	Sheroanawë Hakihiiwë at Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Sheroanawë Hakihiiwë/Fondation Cartier pour l'art contemporain				
					
				

	While the paintings and drawings that Sheroanawë Hakihiiwë produces may look to Western eyes like abstractions, they are, for him, ways of recording the Yanomami culture that he interacts with daily. Working in a remote part of Venezuela, Hakihiiwë takes the jungle around him as his inspiration, often depicting spare trees set against vibrantly hued backgrounds. Minimalist though these works may be, they have made some noise in the Western art world, with New York’s Museum of Modern Art and Italy’s Venice Biennale both showing pieces in recent years. Hakihiiwë will have his first U.S. survey with this exhibition, featuring an animation, an installation, and newly commissioned works.

	November 19–March 28, 2027

		
			
			
	Diane Severin Nguyen at Haus der Kunst, Munich
			
										
					Image Credit: Rockbund Art Museum				
					
				

	Diane Severin Nguyen’s unforgettable 2021 video If Revolution Is a Sickness tracks a Vietnamese child in Warsaw, repeatedly invoking the trauma of the American war in Vietnam, if only obliquely. But the video is not entirely a downer; its finale is a bombastic K-pop-inspired dance routine set to a song written by the artist and Ryder Bach that refers to revolutionary sentiment. The sequence suggests a reconciliation with the pain of the conflict. “We make life through images,” the artist has said of her work. Here, she will debut a new video installation whose vague yet intriguing description notes: “The new film takes flight as the viewer is caught between sky and ground in a moving pursuit. Sentiment merges with machinery and music becomes a force.”

	November 20–May 16, 2027

		
			
			
	Rubaiya Qatar at Various venues, Qatar
			
										
					Image Credit: Qatar Museums				
					
				

	At last, Qatar’s rapidly expanding art scene has a recurring art festival with Rubaiya Qatar, an expo that will take place once every four years. Rather than being a single art exhibition, as most biennials are, Rubaiya Qatar has a more diffuse format, with several mini-shows cohering to form a larger one. The star presentation this time is “Unruly Waters,” a show about Qatar’s position in a globalized world that will take place at the Al Riwaq Art + Architecture pavilion and the Museum of Islamic Art. Alongside it will be such events as a new performance by Rirkrit Tiravanija, who will repeatedly make bread with a range of bakers acting as emissaries from an array of Qatari cultures.

	November 21–April 30, 2027

		
			
			
	“Van Eyck: The Portraits” at National Gallery, London
			
										
					Image Credit: ©National Gallery, London				
					
				

	Sure, the National Gallery has Jan van Eyck’s most famous painting—The Arnolfini Portrait (1434), an iconic work of the Northern Renaissance—but why not enjoy all eight of the Flemish artist’s other portraits alongside it? These nine paintings account for nearly half of all the works that have been concretely attributed solely to Van Eyck; that they have all been convened for this exhibition is nothing short of a small miracle. Seen together, the paintings will display Van Eyck’s fabulous ability to furnish his portraits with a level of detail made possible by his pioneering use of oil paint. His skill is evident in Portrait of a Man, his 1433 painting of a person—perhaps the artist himself—whose eyes are surrounded by highly naturalistic wrinkles.

	November 21–April 11, 2027

		
			
			
	Opening of Kanal, Brussels
			
										
					Image Credit: Photo Bart Grietens/Fondation KANAL Stichting				
					
				

	Kanal, a 430,000-square-foot art complex in a former Citröen garage, has had a particularly difficult road to opening: A Belgian government shutdown threatened its funding, a partnership with Paris’s Centre Pompidou occasionally appeared to fray, and a fire ripped through part of the museum during construction, thankfully with little damage to the structure. Against all odds, Kanal is finally almost here. The museum, which cost an estimated €230 million to build, will kick off with a show that is fittingly titled “A Truly Immense Journey”; included will be 350 works from the Pompidou collection, among them pieces by Henri Matisse and Alberto Giacometti. There’s a playground by Assemble, a Turner Prize–winning architecture group, and performances by Miet Warlop, the transgressive performance artist currently representing Belgium in the Venice Biennale.

	Opens November 28, 2026

		
			
			
	“Pushwagner” at Astrup Fearnley Museum, Oslo
			
										
					Image Credit: Øystein Thorvaldsen/Courtesy Galleri K, Oslo				
					
				

	The graphic novel Soft City (1969–75), Hariton Pushwagner’s magnum opus, is filled with endless rows of anonymous buildings, gibberish murmurings, and giant crowds of people arranged as though they were objects on an assembly line. The book was an implicit critique of capitalism and its obsession with order and was flavored with a kind of quirkiness that ran through all of Pushwagner’s output. (His pseudonym was itself idiosyncratic, translating from the Norwegian to “a ton of Hare Krishna pushwagons”; he was born under the much plainer name of Terje Brofos.) Soft City will be contextualized alongside Pushwagner’s paintings, prints, and friezes contending with dissatisfaction and alienation in this retrospective, the most important one for the Oslo-based artist in Norway since his death in 2018.

	November 28–April 11, 2027
